opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difference comes down to where the learning signal comes from and how general the prior is.

AlphaZero is an incredible result, but it lives in a world with a perfectly specified environment and a crisp reward. You know the rules of Go, you can simulate as many games as you want, and at the end someone wins. That lets you bootstrap from nothing through self-play. The real world doesn't give you that. There's no clean simulator for "be a good software engineer" or "do useful research," and the reward is fuzzy, delayed, and often only definable by humans.

Language models solve the cold-start problem. Pre-training on the internet gives you an enormous, rich prior: a compressed model of how humans reason, write code, argue, plan, and explain things. That gets you a model that can at least *attempt* almost any task. Once a model can sometimes succeed, you can apply RL on top, and suddenly you're in a regime that looks a lot more like AlphaZero. You sample, check which attempts worked, and reinforce those. The prior is what makes the search tractable. Without it you'd be doing random exploration in an impossibly large space and you'd never stumble onto a correct proof or a working program.

So I don't see it as language models *versus* the AlphaZero approach. It's more that language models are the thing that makes the AlphaZero recipe applicable to general domains. The last couple of years have basically shown this. Once RL on verifiable tasks like math and coding started working on top of strong base models, capabilities jumped pretty dramatically.

The other piece is that language is the interface to everything humans care about. Tasks, feedback, tools, and collaboration are all expressible in text, so a model that operates in that medium can plug into the economy in a way a Go engine never could.

r001.rationale: The response describes Go’s specified rules, win/loss outcome, and self-play, but does not clearly identify the setting as two-player and perfect-information.

r002.rationale: It says pretraining provides a broad prior that lets a model attempt many tasks, but does not identify general conceptual understanding of the world as a prerequisite for broader AI.

r003.rationale: It contrasts games’ crisp rewards with real-world tasks’ fuzzy, delayed rewards that are often only definable by humans.

r004.rationale: It says models must sometimes succeed before RL can reinforce attempts that work, and describes checking successes on verifiable real-world tasks such as math and coding.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing is what kind of signal you're learning from. AlphaZero is incredible, right, it's one of the most beautiful results in the field. But it works because Go gives you this perfect, cheap, verifiable reward. You can play millions of games against yourself and every single one of them tells you something true about whether you played well. And the environment is fully specified. There's nothing about the world you need to know to play Go that isn't contained in the rules of Go.

The problem is that almost nothing we actually care about looks like that. If you want a system that can do science, or write software, or negotiate, or just understand what a person means when they ask for something, there's no simulator you can spin up. You can't self-play your way into knowing what a protein is or what the tax code says. That knowledge has to come from somewhere, and the only place it exists in a sufficiently dense form is the record of everything humans have written down.

So the thing language models get you is a prior. Pretraining on the internet is basically a way of compressing a huge fraction of human knowledge and, more importantly, human reasoning patterns into the weights. And once you have that prior, a lot of the problems that looked intractable for the AlphaZero approach get much easier. You don't need to learn from scratch what a good move looks like in an open-ended domain, because the model already has a decent guess. Then you can layer the RL on top. That's where I think it gets really exciting, actually, because you get to keep most of what made AlphaZero work. You still want verifiable rewards, you still want the model to search and improve on its own judgment. You're just starting from something that already knows a lot about the world rather than from random weights.

And there's a second thing, which is that language is also the interface. The reason it's so useful is that it's the medium humans use to specify tasks, to give feedback, to explain why something went wrong. An AlphaZero-style system that was superhuman at some narrow thing would still have this enormous gap between its capability and our ability to direct it. A language model you can just talk to. You can say "no, do it this way," and it can update. That's a really underrated property if what you want is something general.

So I'd put it as: AlphaZero showed you what's possible when you have a clean reward and unlimited compute in one domain. Language models are the thing that let you take that recipe and point it at the messy, open-ended world. I don't think it's either-or. I think the actual path is language models as the substrate, with the AlphaZero ideas as the engine you run on top of them.

r001.rationale: The response describes Go as fully specified and its rewards as verifiable, but does not identify the setting as two-player and perfect-information.

r002.rationale: It says pretraining provides a prior containing human knowledge and reasoning, so the model starts with knowledge of the world for open-ended tasks.

r003.rationale: It contrasts Go’s cheap, verifiable reward with real-world tasks that lack a simulator and cannot be learned through self-play in the same way.

r004.rationale: It says to layer reinforcement learning on top of a pretrained prior and retain verifiable rewards, but does not identify access to an initial real-world reward signal as the foothold for improvement.

astra-6.text:
I think the key difference is the breadth of what you’re learning from. AlphaZero is incredibly impressive, but it operates in a closed environment: you have a fixed set of rules, a clear reward signal, and you can generate as much experience as you want through self-play. The hard part is figuring out how to take that recipe and apply it to the rest of the world, where you don’t necessarily have any of those things.

With language models, you’re starting with this enormous collection of human knowledge and reasoning. To predict text well, you have to learn something about all the processes that produced it—people’s intentions, how the physical world works, how to write a program, how to construct an argument. So the training objective is simple, but the range of capabilities it pushes you toward is much broader.

That doesn’t mean prediction alone necessarily gets you all the way to AGI. You probably want systems that can act, experiment, and learn from whether their actions worked. But a language model gives you a very useful starting point for that. You can then bring in reinforcement learning and some of the ideas that made AlphaZero successful, with a system that already knows quite a lot about the world.

r001.rationale: The response describes AlphaZero as operating in a closed environment with fixed rules and a clear reward, but does not identify its two-player, perfect-information game setting.

r002.rationale: It says language models learn broad knowledge, including how the physical world works, and provide a useful starting point for systems that act and learn beyond AlphaZero’s closed setting.

r003.rationale: It contrasts AlphaZero’s clear reward signal with the real world, where one may not have such a signal, communicating that real-world rewards are harder to specify.

r004.rationale: It mentions learning from whether actions worked and adding reinforcement learning, but does not state that access to an initial real-world reward signal is the foothold for beginning that improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
The thing that made AlphaZero so compelling was that you could start with almost nothing, give it a way to play against itself, and get superhuman performance. But a huge amount of the problem is specified for you: here are the legal moves, here’s the board, here’s what it means to win. The hard question is how you get that kind of learning to work in the real world, where you don’t have such a clean environment or reward signal.

Language gives you this incredibly rich starting point. People have written down how they reason about things, how they solve problems, what happened when they tried something. Predicting that text pushes a model to learn a much broader set of capabilities than playing a particular game does. And you can train on an enormous amount of it without having to construct an environment for every skill you want.

I don’t think that means the AlphaZero idea is wrong. The exciting thing is combining them: use language modeling to get a broad base of knowledge and capabilities, then use reinforcement learning to let the model practice, explore, and discover things beyond what people have written down. Pretraining gives you a starting point from which that process seems much more likely to work.

r001.rationale: It describes AlphaZero’s clean game setup, legal moves, board, and win condition, but does not identify the setting as two-player and perfect-information.

r002.rationale: It says language pretraining provides broad knowledge and capabilities, but does not clearly state that general conceptual understanding of the world is a prerequisite for developing more general AI.

r003.rationale: It says real-world tasks lack a clean environment or reward signal, directly identifying real-world reward signals as harder to specify than game rewards.

r004.rationale: It discusses using reinforcement learning to practice, explore, and discover, but does not identify access to an initial real-world reward signal as the foothold for that improvement.
